algebra.title: Boolean algebra rules
algebra.intro: These rules let you rewrite a DNF into shorter equivalent forms. They power the step-by-step solution path and the worked examples in the simulator.

identity.name: Identity
identity.example: 1 acts as the neutral element of ∧ and 0 as the neutral element of ∨.

domination.name: Domination
domination.example: Whatever is OR-ed with 1 is forced to 1; whatever is AND-ed with 0 is forced to 0.

idempotence.name: Idempotence
idempotence.example: Repeating the same operand neither tightens nor relaxes the term.

double_negation.name: Double negation
double_negation.example: Two negations cancel each other out.

complement.name: Complement
complement.example: A variable is always either true or false — so a ∨ ¬a is always 1, and a ∧ ¬a is always 0.

commutativity.name: Commutativity
commutativity.example: Operand order does not affect the result for ∧ and ∨.

associativity.name: Associativity
associativity.example: With multiple ∧ or ∨ operations, the grouping does not matter — (a ∧ b) ∧ c equals a ∧ (b ∧ c).

distributivity.name: Distributivity
distributivity.example: A shared operand can be factored out — like factoring in regular maths, but with ∧ and ∨ instead of · and +.

absorption.name: Absorption
absorption.example: If a is already true, then a ∨ (a ∧ b) is also true — the AND part adds nothing.

de_morgan.name: De Morgan
de_morgan.example: Negation flips the operator: ∧ becomes ∨ and each operand is negated.

exercise.solutionHint: The full solution can now be shown as the final hint.
exercise.simplificationHint: Use the Boolean algebra rules (absorption, distributivity, complement, …) to bring the DNF into a shorter equivalent form.
exercise.minimalDnfNote: {{literalsLabel}} in {{termsLabel}} — DNF form (OR of AND-terms), e.g. result of Quine-McCluskey.
exercise.factoredNote: {{literalsLabel}} — shorter than the minimal DNF and mathematically equivalent, but no longer in DNF form.
exercise.factoredFallbackNote: {{literalsLabel}} — equivalent and shorter than the minimal DNF. For more than 4 variables, this form is not guaranteed to be globally minimal.
exercise.walkthroughNote: This path is not unique. It shows one possible grouping of the 1-rows into a minimal form.
exercise.walkthroughRowsText: Rows {{rows}} provide the terms of the correct DNF.
exercise.walkthroughNoRows: There is no 1-row; the function is 0 for every assignment.
exercise.walkthroughAllRows: All rows have result 1, so the whole DNF can be collapsed to 1.
exercise.walkthroughAlwaysFalse: Without a 1-row, no AND group remains. The minimal form is therefore 0.
exercise.walkthroughGroupsIntro: Each group below shows how its 1-rows reduce step by step to a shorter term — distributivity factors out the shared literals, the complement rule collapses (x ∨ ¬x) to 1, and the identity rule drops the trailing ∧ 1.
exercise.walkthroughGroupNoEliminated: Already a single term — no reduction needed.
exercise.walkthroughCoverText: The selected groups cover all 1-rows — no 1-row is left over.
exercise.walkthroughFactoredText: The minimal DNF has {{minimalLiterals}} literals. The shorter equivalent form needs only {{factoredLiterals}} literals — but the DNF form is lost.
exercise.walkthroughFactoredNote: This form is mathematically equivalent but no longer a DNF. When it comes from factoring, the distributivity steps are shown as well.
exercise.walkthroughFactoredFallbackTitle: Optional: best found form outside DNF
exercise.walkthroughFactoredFallbackText: The minimal DNF has {{minimalLiterals}} literals. The found equivalent form needs only {{factoredLiterals}} literals — but the DNF form is lost.
exercise.walkthroughFactoredFallbackNote: For more than 4 variables, the safe fallback is used here. The form is correct and simplified, but it is not guaranteed to be the globally shortest boolean formula.
